details: Distribution coefficient Kd: ratio of sorbed activity per unit dry mass to dissolved activity per unit volume; Kd = (Bq/kg_soil) / (Bq/L_water); unit: L/kg; Cs-137 in mineral soils: Kd = 1,000-100,000 L/kg (illite clay dominant sorption via FES = frayed edge sites on clay minerals); Sr-90 in mineral soils: Kd = 1-100 L/kg (exchangeable Ca-analog; weak sorption); retardation factor R = 1 + (ρ_bulk/θ)×Kd where ρ_bulk = soil bulk density (~1.5 g/cm³) and θ = volumetric water content (~0.3); effective velocity v_eff = v_water / R; Cs-137 R = 1 + (1.5/0.3)×10,000 = 50,001 → essentially immobile (v_eff = v_water / 50,001)
chernobyl_application: Cs-137 in CEZ soils: Kd typically 5,000-50,000 L/kg in clay-containing mineral soils; R > 10,000; effective velocity ~0.001-0.01 cm/yr; confirms observed depth profile: >90% still in top 5 cm after 40yr; Sr-90: Kd = 1-20 L/kg in sandy soils; R = 6-100; effective velocity 0.1-1 cm/yr → observed migration 5-40 cm depth (≈consistent); ratio Kd_Cs/Kd_Sr = ~100-1000 → explains why Cs-137 stays at surface while Sr-90 reaches groundwater; key for understanding which contaminated areas pose ongoing groundwater threat vs surface exposure
source: Cremers 1988 Nature doi:10.1038/340563a0; Bossew 2001 J Environ Radioact; Kashparov 2003; Bulgakov 2002; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv; chernobyl_groundwater_contamination_REAL.csv

details: Frayed Edge Sites (FES) on illite and vermiculite clay minerals: primary mechanism for Cs-137 high Kd; FES are defects at edges of 2:1 layer silicates where interlayer K⁺ has been lost → exposed sites with very high selectivity for Cs⁺ (and NH4⁺); selectivity coefficient K_c(Cs/K) on FES = 1000-10,000 (Cs outcompetes K by 3-4 orders of magnitude); FES occupy ~0.01-0.1% of total clay surface but account for >90% of Cs adsorption; FES density = ~2×10⁻⁶ mol/kg illite; once sorbed: Cs extremely difficult to desorb (irreversible on decadal timescale); explains why K-fertilizer REDUCES Cs uptake: K⁺ competes for transport across root membrane but Cs is already largely immobilized in FES
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl implication: Cs-137 deposited 1986 has been progressively incorporated into FES of illite minerals → becoming more immobile over time ('fixation'); first 1-2 years: exchangeable fraction higher; after 5-10 years: predominantly fixed; Kd increases over time = aging effect; consequence: decontamination of Cs-137 from soil becomes HARDER with time (more firmly bound); K-fertilizer reduces plant uptake 2-10x by competing at root surface (not soil) even if soil Kd stays high; Cs-137 remains essentially a surface contamination marker for centuries
source: Cremers 1988; Rigol 2002 J Environ Radioact; Evans 1983; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv; decontamination_countermeasures_REAL.csv

details: Cs-137 vertical migration in CEZ soils (observed 2016-2026): undisturbed soil profiles: >90% of Cs-137 still in top 5 cm (plowing zone depth not reached naturally); depth profile: exponential decrease with depth scale ~2-3 cm; migration rate ~0.1-0.3 cm/yr in sandy CEZ soils; in peat bogs: variable (organic matter complexes Cs but peat accumulation can bury Cs with ~0.3-1.0 cm/yr peat growth); in forest litter: biological cycling important (fungal hyphae = primary pathway; mycorrhizal networks redistribute Cs); disturbed soils (plowed): Cs-137 homogenized in plow layer 0-20 cm = agricultural decontamination model failed
chernobyl_application: Anthropogenic bioturbation (1990s decontamination plowing) actually redistributed Cs-137 from surface 0-5 cm to 0-20 cm layer → reduced surface dose rate (≈5-10x) but increased root zone contamination (increased plant uptake); earthworm bioturbation 1-5 cm/yr can slowly redistribute some Cs; fungal hyphae redistribute between organic horizons; 2022 Russian military vehicle traffic in CEZ: tread marks disrupted soil crust → localized resuspension; Red Forest: 2022 Russian trenches dug through Cs-137/Sr-90 contaminated burial sites → groundwater contamination concern; IAEA post-occupation inspection found no significant aquifer contamination from this
source: Klosowski 2015 J Environ Radioact; Bossew 2001; Yoshida 1998; red_forest_waste_sites_REAL.csv; cez_research_2022_2025_REAL.csv

details: Sr-90 vertical migration in CEZ soils: Kd = 1-20 L/kg (sandy soil); R = 6-100 (Sandy CEZ soils); effective transport velocity = 0.1-1.5 cm/yr; observed depth profiles 2010-2020: peak Sr-90 at 5-25 cm in sandy soils (consistent with 24-40 cm total migration over 35+ years at 0.7-1.2 cm/yr); maximum activity concentration still in top 0-5 cm layer in most profiles but with substantial tail to 25-40 cm; in sandy aquifer recharge zones: Sr-90 has reached water table (1-5 m depth) at multiple CEZ monitoring wells; fuel particle dissolution releasing Sr-90 at original deposition depth = additional input below original surface layer
chernobyl_application: Sr-90 groundwater contamination worst near: (1) Red Forest burial trenches (liquid waste + solid debris in trenches → leaching); (2) Vehicle graveyard Rossokha; (3) Cooling pond drawdown areas; (4) Near-field fuel particle deposition zones (NW direction 1-10 km); Sr-90 in Pripyat River: elevated in springs (snowmelt mobilizes more) and after wildfires (disrupts soil structure; increases lateral flow); 2020 post-wildfire peak 11 Bq/L Pripyat River (May 2021 peak); WHO guideline 10 Bq/L exceeded during post-wildfire and flooding events

details: Peat bog radionuclide behavior: peat soils (>30% organic carbon): Cs-137 retention different from mineral soils; organic matter provides cation exchange sites but NOT FES (no clay minerals in pure peat); Kd for Cs-137 in peat: 100-5000 L/kg (lower than mineral soil FES) but organic complexation creates high affinity sorption; Sr-90 in peat: Kd = 0.5-5 L/kg (lower than mineral soil = more mobile); peat physical structure: vertical transport dominated by hydraulic conductivity gradient; lateral transport via surface runoff in heavy rain; peat in CEZ: Pripyat River floodplain; northern CEZ bog systems; peat bogs = Cs-137 concentrating systems (accumulate from atmospheric deposition + runoff); lichen→peat transfer coefficient = pathway to reindeer
chernobyl_application: Belarus peat deposits: highest contamination concentration per kg in some peat profiles; peat harvesting for fuel (traditional in Belarus) = radiological concern; peat dust inhalation during mechanical harvest = hot particle inhalation pathway; Belarus peat-fuel combustion near Chernobyl zone → Cs-137 atmospheric resuspension; peat fire resuspension (2020): peat contains concentrated Cs-137 accumulated over 35 years of spring flooding/deposition; peat bog Cs-137 = long-term secondary reservoir for future wildfire resuspension events on 100-200 year timescale
source: Konopleva 2009 J Environ Radioact; Zibold 2001; wildfire_resuspension_REAL.csv; cez_ecosystem_ecology_REAL.csv

details: Pu-239 and Am-241 depth profiles: CEZ soils: >99% of Pu-239 in top 5 cm (2026); Am-241 follows Pu distribution (in-growth from Pu-241 at same locations); Pu Kd = 50,000-500,000 L/kg in mineral soil (essentially immobile due to: low solubility of PuO2; strong sorption; plutonium fuel particles not yet fully dissolved); effective migration of dissolved Pu: <0.01 cm/yr; Pu in groundwater: below detection in most CEZ monitoring wells; exception: locations with high organic carbon mobilizing colloidal Pu; Am-241 Kd = 1,000-100,000 L/kg; colloidal transport possible but rare
chernobyl_application: Pu-239/240 in CEZ: estimated inventory 3.5 PBq in top 10 cm of soil over 125,000 km² contaminated area; hot spots near NPP: 4-150 µm fuel particles with Pu concentration factor 1000x vs surrounding soil; fuel particle dissolution half-time 5-25yr (Type II/III particles from cladding breached fuel) → ongoing Pu dissolution from particle matrix; dissolved Pu: rapidly re-sorbs (Kd>>10,000) = self-immobilizing; Pu in CEZ = essentially permanent on human timescale (Pu-239 t½=24,110yr; Kd immobility = permanent); Am-241 growing in same depth profile = increasingly alpha-active surface layer
source: Kashparov 2003; Oughton 1997 J Environ Radioact; am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv; fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv

details: Soil type effect on radionuclide plant transfer: transfer factor (TF = Bq/kg plant / Bq/kg soil) varies by soil type; Cs-137 TF comparison: sandy soil (low clay; low K; low organic): TF = 0.01-0.5; clay soil (illite; high K; FES abundant): TF = 0.001-0.05; organic-rich/peat: TF = 0.05-2.0; ratio sandy:clay TF ≈ 10-100x; Sr-90 TF comparison: sandy soil (low Ca; low clay): TF = 0.1-5; clay soil (Ca-rich): TF = 0.01-0.5; ratio sandy:clay ≈ 5-10x; CEZ soil types: northern CEZ = Quaternary sandy podzols (high TF); southern CEZ near NPP = loamy; Black Sea watershed = mixed
chernobyl_application: Near-CEZ agricultural land (outer zones): predominantly sandy Quaternary soils = HIGHEST TF; explains Ukrainian grain Sr-90 exceedances: 45% of 2011-2019 samples exceeded 20 Bq/kg in near-CEZ farming areas despite low soil contamination overall; K fertilizer (300-500 kg KCl/ha/yr) reduces Cs-137 TF by 33-50% but does not reduce Sr-90 (different element; Ca-fertilizer/liming needed for Sr-90); liming increases pH → reduces Sr-90 solubility in soil solution; combined K+Ca/lime application = most effective countermeasure reducing both Cs-137 and Sr-90 TF by 50-80%
source: Nisbet 1992 J Environ Radioact; Howard 2001; ukraine_crop_contamination_REAL.csv; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv; decontamination_countermeasures_REAL.csv

details: Fuel particle dissolution and radionuclide release: hot particle types: Type I = high-temperature oxide (UO2+x; crystalline; 5-25yr dissolution half-time); Type II = silicate matrix (glass-like; 50-200yr dissolution half-time); Type III = metallic/carbide (faster dissolution; <5yr); dissolution releases radionuclides at variable rates; dissolution model: dC/dt = -λ_diss × C_particle (first-order); λ_diss = ln2/t½_diss; for Type I: λ_diss = 0.028-0.139/yr; for UO2 dissolution: U-235 and Pu-239 released but rapidly re-sorb on soil (Kd>>10,000); Sr-90 released moves into soil solution (Kd=1-20) → available for plant uptake and groundwater migration
chernobyl_application: Red Forest 2015 survey: still 31% of local inventory in Type I particles (Kashparov 2003 estimate updated); 40 years of weathering: significant dissolution has occurred but Type I particles = persistent source term for decades more; practical consequence: Sr-90 leaching from particle dissolution continues feeding groundwater contamination; Cs-137 released from particles = immobilized by FES (irrelevant to groundwater); Pu-239 released from particles = immobilized by soil; Sr-90 = the only radionuclide whose particle dissolution actually matters for groundwater pathway; IAEA fuel particle monitoring program tracks this
